PRODSECRM-312.summary: Add trusted third-party RPM signature verification keys to Conforma's global allowed_list (Mellanox, Habanalabs/Intel, CentOS, Intel OpenVINO, Fedora/EPEL)
PRODSECRM-312.description:
Exception Title: Add trusted third-party RPM signature verification keys to Conforma's global allowed_list (Mellanox, Habanalabs/Intel, CentOS, Intel OpenVINO, Fedora/EPEL)
Exception Type: Conforma - Konflux/ EC policy check, blocking release
Business Unit: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
Product: Red Hat OpenShift AI (RHOAI)
Conforma MR Link: No new MR for this request — this is a policy question asking whether these keys can be added to Conforma's global allowed_list. Background/precedent: https://gitlab.cee.redhat.com/releng/konflux-release-data/-/merge_requests/19223 (consolidated MR covering the existing per-release exceptions for these same keys).
Exception Reason:
RHOAI ships components built on third-party base images/RPM repos (AMD ROCm, Mellanox, Habanalabs/Intel, CentOS, Intel OpenVINO, Fedora/EPEL) that are covered by existing Red Hat vendor legal agreements (https://www.redhat.com/en/about/third-party-end-user-agreements). Conforma's rpm_signature.allowed check currently requires a per-component, per-release, time-boxed exception MR for each of these already-known, already-legally-cleared vendor keys, resulting in repeated PSX/PRODSECRM tickets for the same keys release after release (e.g. https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/PSX-1098#icft=PSX-1098
, https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/PSX-1099#icft=PSX-1099
, https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/PSX-1101#icft=PSX-1101
, https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/PSX-1106#icft=PSX-1106
, https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/PSX-1110#icft=PSX-1110
). AMD's and NVIDIA's keys were recently converted to permanent standing exceptions directly in the RHOAI EnterpriseContractPolicy (see consolidated MR https://gitlab.cee.redhat.com/releng/konflux-release-data/-/merge_requests/19223). We are asking ProdSec to confirm whether the remaining known, legally-cleared verification keys (Mellanox a024f6f0e6d6a281, Habanalabs/Intel 910ea37ba2d18d0c, CentOS 05b555b38483c65d, Intel OpenVINO 28da432daac8baea, Fedora/EPEL 8a3872bf3228467c) can instead be added to Conforma's global allowed_list, removing the recurring exception overhead going forward. This is a request to avoid needing exceptions in the future, not a request to approve a new policy violation.
Risk of Approving Exception:
If these specific, already-legally-cleared verification keys are added to the global allowed list, any Konflux-onboarded team could rely on RPMs signed with these vendor keys without a policy check, i.e. the control becomes global instead of scoped to RHOAI's specific, vetted components. Per Austin Kimbrell (ProdSec), Conforma currently has no mechanism to scope an allowed key to specific teams/projects only - it is all-or-nothing for everyone.
Impact if Exception NOT Approved:
Status quo continues: RHOAI must keep filing a new time-boxed Conforma exception (with a new PSX/PRODSECRM ticket) for the same known vendor keys every time a release or z-stream needs one, repeating review overhead ProdSec has already granted multiple times for the same keys, with no reduction in ongoing process burden for either RHOAI or ProdSec.
Proposed Remediation:
If approved: Release Engineering adds the approved keys to Conforma's global allowed_list (e.g. rule_data.allowed_rpm_signature_keys or equivalent global data source), and the existing per-release PSX/PRODSECRM exception tickets for those keys can be closed as no longer needed. If declined: this ticket is closed for documentation purposes only, and RHOAI continues the existing per-release Conforma exception process, referencing this ticket for context.
Approving VP Email: jofernan@redhat.com
Exception Expiration: 9/7/2027
Additional Watchers: akimbrel@redhat.com, ckodama@redhat.com, wznoinsk@redhat.com, lmohanty@redhat.com, saberry@redhat.com, ansyed@redhat.com
Related Risk Ticket: N/A

PSX-1106.description:
Control
Conforma Enterprise Contract policy rule: rpm_signature.allowed:910ea37ba2d18d0c (Habanalabs/Intel RPM signing key)
Scope of Exception
odh-vllm-gaudi container image; 4 Habanalabs RPMs (habanalabs-rdma-core, habanalabs-thunk, habanalabs-graph, habanalabs-firmware-tools) per version, 2 RHOAI versions affected (rhoai-2.25, rhoai-3.3).
Konflux component names: odh-vllm-gaudi-v2-25, odh-vllm-gaudi-v3-3
Accepting Risks?
RPMs signed with Habanalabs key (910ea37ba2d18d0c) rather than Red Hat key. Acceptable because Habanalabs (Intel) is a trusted partner with a legal agreement in progress. The RPMs provide hardware acceleration support for Intel Gaudi AI accelerator cards.
Description
RHOAI ships the odh-vllm-gaudi container image which provides vLLM inference support on Intel Gaudi accelerator hardware. This image includes 4 RPMs from Habanalabs (now part of Intel) that are signed with the Habanalabs GPG key 910ea37ba2d18d0c rather than a Red Hat key. These RPMs provide essential driver and firmware support (RDMA core, thunk, graph compiler, firmware tools) for the Gaudi hardware.
Legal agreements to formally allow use of these Habanalabs-signed RPMs are being tracked in RHOAIENG-38427.
Proposal (Remediation)
Legal agreement with Habanalabs/Intel is being tracked. Once signed, RPMs will be properly onboarded or re-signed with an approved key. Exception will be removed once the legal framework is in place.
Impact of not approving
RHOAI releases containing Intel Gaudi/Habanalabs accelerator support cannot ship. vLLM workloads on Gaudi hardware would be blocked for all customers with Intel Gaudi accelerators. Affected versions: rhoai-2.25, rhoai-3.3.

RHAISTRAT-576.description:
Problem Statement
Third-party vendor packages used in Red Hat OpenShift AI (RHOAI) product images are being flagged by release gating processes as causing license or compliance violations. These violations prevent affected images from being pushed to the official registry, blocking product releases and creating compliance risks.
This feature addresses the need to systematically identify, validate, and resolve all third-party package compliance issues to ensure all product images meet Red Hat's release requirements and can be successfully published.
Objectives
- Identify all third-party RPMs and packages causing compliance violations

- Ensure traceability of all impacted images, RPMs, and components

- Validate package sources and establish Red Hat-compliant alternatives

- Obtain necessary legal approvals for packages that cannot be replaced

- Establish a process to prevent future compliance violations

Implementation Plan
Step 1: Identify RPM Usage
Provide a detailed breakdown of all RPMs used by each image impacted by license or compliance violations.
_ _Status*: Spike work driving next steps
_ _Owner*: @wznoinsk
_ _Related Task*: RHOAIENG-38497
Step 2: Update Vendor Epics
Update every related "Vendor" epic to include all identified images, RPMs, and impacted components for traceability.
- Create comprehensive mapping of violations to epics

- Document all affected images and their dependencies

- Establish clear traceability chain

Step 3: Validate Package Sources
For each RPM, create a dedicated task to verify whether the package can be:
- Installed from Red Hat–signed sources, OR

- Built from source code

_ _Decision Point*: If neither option is possible, a legal agreement will be required.
Step 4: Analyze Remaining Gaps
Based on the results from Step 3, identify all components and images that cannot be built using:
- Red Hat–provided packages, OR

- Source builds (including those based on consuming AIPCC content if those violate Konflux enterprise contract on RHOAI site)

Step 5: Legal Follow-up
Share the list of non-compliant components/images with the Legal team to initiate:
- Approval processes for external sources

- Licensing agreements where required

- Documentation of approved exceptions

Success Criteria
- All RPMs causing violations are identified and documented

- All vendor epics are updated with complete traceability information

- Package source validation is completed for all flagged RPMs

- Legal approvals are obtained for all non-compliant packages

- All product images can be successfully pushed to official registry

- Release gating processes pass without compliance violations

Dependencies
- Completion of spike work (https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHOAIENG-38497#icft=RHOAIENG-38497
)

- Access to package source information

- Legal team availability for review and approval processes

- Vendor epic owners for updates

Risks
- Some packages may require lengthy legal approval processes

- Replacing non-compliant packages may impact functionality

- Timeline dependencies on external legal review

- Potential need to modify build processes for source-based alternatives

RHOAIENG-38497.description:
Objective
This spike task is the first step in addressing third-party package compliance violations that are blocking product images from being pushed to the official registry. The goal is to provide a comprehensive breakdown of all RPMs used by each image that has been flagged for license or compliance violations.
Context
Third-party vendor packages in Red Hat OpenShift AI (RHOAI) product images are being flagged by release gating processes as causing license or compliance violations. These violations prevent affected images from being pushed to the official registry, blocking product releases.
This spike work will drive the next steps in the compliance remediation process outlined in RHOAISTRAT-766.
Scope
Identify and document:
- All images that have been flagged for license or compliance violations

- Complete list of RPMs used by each flagged image

- Package versions and sources for each RPM

- Mapping of RPMs to their respective images

- Any dependencies or relationships between packages

Deliverables
- Comprehensive inventory document/spreadsheet containing: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1o2j87H-k33eBsDcxR4oeqpNJJZe_TqHarnEBw-PqepM/edit?gid=1354667519#gid=1354667519
__ Image name and registry location
__ Complete list of RPMs per image
__ RPM version information
__ Package source information (where available)
__ Violation type/category for each flagged package

- Structured data format that can be used for:
__ Updating vendor epics (Step 2)
__ Creating validation tasks (Step 3)
__ Gap analysis (Step 4)
__ Legal review (Step 5)

Approach
- Review release gating reports and violation logs

- Analyze container images and their package manifests

- Extract RPM information from build artifacts

- Cross-reference with known violation databases

- Document findings in a structured format

Success Criteria
- All flagged images are identified

- Complete RPM inventory is documented for each image

- Data is structured and ready for use in subsequent steps

- Traceability is established between images, RPMs, and violations

Dependencies
- Access to release gating reports and violation data

- Access to container image manifests and build artifacts

- Access to package databases and version information

Related Work
- Parent Feature: RHOAISTRAT-766 - AI Platform – Third-Party Content Compliance & Release Requirements

comments.author: Christian Heimes
comments.body: The ticket lists RHEL 8 and RHEL 9 packages as well as old ROCm 6.x package. We do neither support RHEL 8 nor ROCm 6. For RHOAI 3.5, we are providing base images with ROCm 7 (AFAIK 7.1 or 7.14).

comments.author: Lance Barto
comments.body:
@Waldemar Znoinski To the best of my knowledge, as stated by Christian we are only supporting RHEL9 ROCm 7.14 base images for 3.5. 

I don’t think that any of these RPMs will be in scope for us to support or to add into that base image. You’re likely going to need prodsec exemptions for these RPMs until you’re able to upgrade to what we support and we can then work towards onboarding your team to the base image we produce (and add missing RPMs that you may need to that base image)

comments.author: Lance Barto
Lance Barto
comments.body: @Waldemar Znoinski Please acknowledge the comment below, and we will close the ticket.

comments.author: Doug Hellmann
comments.body: @Waldemar Znoinski and @Lance Barto , please update the description of this ticket (or make a new one?) with only the packages that need work. Focus on identifying the latest versions, including if any are in the mirror already but we need a newer version than we are mirroring.

comments.author: Lance Barto
comments.body:
Not hearing anything from @Waldemar Znoinski about this in over a week; I’m closing the ticket as all the RPMs above are either built or mirrored by AIPCC today.

As each component team onboards their builds to AIPCC they’ll have the opportunity to identify and request missing RPMS as needed.

PSX-1097.description:
Note: Important Dates (Jira fields)
- Due Date - 2027-05-03 (rhoai-2.25 support end + 7 days)

- Risk Identified Date - 2025-05-01


What is the reason for the exception?
Provide a detailed description explaining why the exception is needed. Please include any technical, resource, historic, or contextual information that can help expedite the review process.

RHOAI workbench and pipeline images for AMD GPU support include ROCm stack packages (hip-runtime, rocblas, miopen-hip, etc.) sourced from AMD. These RPMs are signed with AMD's GPG key 9386b48a1a693c5c which is not in the Conforma allowed_rpm_signature_keys list.
Affected RHOAI versions: 2.25, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5-ea.1. These versions have already been released or are in code-freeze, therefore the violation cannot be fixed retroactively. Adding new signing keys to the global allowed list is not possible — exceptions must be granted per-component via the Conforma exception MR process.
Affected components (6 total): odh-workbench-jupyter-tensorflow-rocm-py312, odh-workbench-jupyter-pytorch-rocm-py312, odh-workbench-jupyter-minimal-rocm-py312, odh-training-rocm62-torch25-py311, odh-pipeline-runtime-tensorflow-rocm-py312, odh-pipeline-runtime-pytorch-rocm-py312 (with version suffixes per RHOAI release).
RHOAIENG tracking ticket: https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHOAIENG-38426
 
Risk if we approve the exception?
E.g. This system currently has shared credentials for all of its users. Delaying this work will make it so an attacker could use the shared credentials and we would not know where the attack originated.

AMD RPM packages are signed with a legitimate AMD GPG key (9386b48a1a693c5c). The key is valid and owned by AMD — it is simply not yet in the Conforma allowed signing keys list. The risk of accepting these packages is minimal as: (1) the packages originate from AMD's official distribution channel, (2) the GPG signature is valid and verifiable, (3) legal agreements for use of these AMD packages are being tracked as part of RHOAIENG-38426.
 
Impact of NOT approving the exception?
Provide details on the impact that not approving this exception will have on your team or product.

Without this exception, Conforma will block release pipeline gates for all affected RHOAI versions (2.25, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5-ea.1). This would prevent z-stream security fixes from shipping and block the 3.5-ea.1 release from proceeding. The AMD GPU workbench images are critical for customers running GPU-accelerated ML workloads on AMD hardware.
 
Proposed remediation
Provide a detailed description of the proposed plan to complete this work.
Additional Notes (optional)
Provide any additional notes or contextual information that can help Product Security better understand this request.

1. Grant Conforma exception for rpm_signature.allowed:9386b48a1a693c5c for affected components for the duration of each release's support lifecycle.
2. For future RHOAI releases, the exception will be requested as part of the release exception MR process if AMD RPMs with this signing key continue to be included.
Separate GitLab MRs are being created for each RHOAI version in https://gitlab.cee.redhat.com/releng/konflux-release-data
